title: Query complexity of directed acyclicity testing with bidirectional access
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty\) for each fixed degree bound \(d\ge 1\) and fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), the minimum worst-case number \(Q(n,d,\varepsilon )\) of incidence-list queries needed by an adaptive randomized two-sided-error tester to distinguish acyclic n-vertex digraphs from digraphs more than \(\varepsilon dn\) edge deletions away from acyclic, when every indegree and outdegree is at most d and both incoming and outgoing queries are allowed.
why: Measures how much local information is needed to certify the absence of global directed cyclic structure up to a proximity promise. It would clarify the power of adaptive two-direction exploration in sparse directed graphs.
status_note: Original access model, distance convention and subsequent related bounds checked through 11 September 2026; no matching sharp query classification found. The card explicitly chooses query complexity as the measure of the source’s best-algorithm question. The 2026 paper was checked at introductory-statement level, not independently proved.

progress.text: Ron asks for the best tester in the directed bidirectional bounded-degree model and reports the earlier \(\Omega (n^{1/3})\) two-sided lower bound.
Peng and Wang explicitly retain that historical bidirectional acyclicity lower bound while studying the relation between two graph-access models.
Yoshida states improved lower bounds for outgoing-only access with bounded outdegree but unrestricted indegree. They are not transferred to this model.

sentences: The graph is directed and has bounded incoming and outgoing degree.
A tester can ask for individual incoming or outgoing neighbors of any labeled vertex.
It must distinguish graphs without directed cycles from graphs requiring more than \(\varepsilon dn\) arc deletions to remove all directed cycles.
The target is the optimal number of adaptive queries with error probability at most one third on either promised case.
Recent lower bounds for outgoing-only access use a different model and do not by themselves settle this bidirectional question.

definitions: The graph is a finite loopless directed graph with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); opposite arcs are allowed, but parallel copies of an arc are not. An oracle query specifies a vertex v, a direction IN or OUT, and an index \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,d\}\); it returns the ith neighbor in that direction or a null symbol if the slot is empty. Lists are consistent with one fixed graph and have arbitrary fixed order, so correctness must hold for every permitted ordering. Vertex labels, n,d and \(\varepsilon\) are given to the tester; it may choose any vertex label, use independent fair random bits, and adapt future queries to previous answers. Internal computation is not charged to query complexity. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{k}, k\ge 2\), with arcs \(v_{i}\to v_{i+1}\) and \(v_{k}\to v_{1}\); acyclic means no such cycle exists. Let \(\tau (G)\) be the minimum number of arcs whose deletion makes G acyclic. An input is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(\tau (G)>\varepsilon dn\). Additions cannot remove cycles, so this agrees with the minimum-edge-edit convention for this property. The tester must accept each acyclic graph with probability at least \(2/3\) and reject each \(\varepsilon\)-far graph with probability at least \(2/3\). There is no guarantee for graphs between these cases. Q is the least integer query bound attainable on all n-vertex inputs and all random branches by a randomized query procedure with these guarantees. An upper-bound family must be generated by a uniform algorithm from n,d and the binary encoding of rational \(\varepsilon\); there is no running-time requirement beyond termination. The requested \(\Theta\) bounds concern growth in n, with constants allowed to depend on the fixed d and \(\varepsilon\). One-sided error, which must always accept acyclic inputs, is a separate restriction.
answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic bound \(F(n,d,\varepsilon ), a\) uniform tester using \(O(F)\) queries, and a matching \(\Omega (F)\) lower bound for the same adaptive two-sided, bidirectional model, for each fixed \(d,\varepsilon\) in the stated range. Hidden constants may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but no factor growing with n may be left unmatched. The source’s broad best-algorithm question is made precise here as optimal query complexity; total runtime is not the cost being classified.

context_blocks.title: A local test of a global obstruction
context_blocks.text: A long directed cycle can remain invisible in a small explored neighborhood. The tester sees only chosen incident edges, so even the ability to move both forward and backward does not directly reveal whether some distant portion closes a cycle.

context_blocks.title: One cycle is not necessarily far from acyclic
context_blocks.text: A directed cycle on n vertices becomes acyclic after deleting one arc. Its normalized distance is \(1/(dn)\), so for fixed positive \(\varepsilon\) and large n it is outside the promised far case. Property testing asks for reliable rejection only when many arc deletions are unavoidable.

context_blocks.title: Historical lower bound and the full-exploration upper bound
context_blocks.text: The source records an \(\Omega (n^{1/3})\) query lower bound for adaptive two-sided testing at suitable fixed parameters. Reading every outgoing list uses at most nd queries and determines the whole graph. The gap between such lower bounds and the linear bound motivates the sharp query question.

context_blocks.title: The oracle changes the strength of a lower bound
context_blocks.text: The 2023 model comparison distinguishes access to both directions from access only to outgoing arcs. A lower bound against the less informative oracle cannot automatically rule out an algorithm with incoming queries.

context_blocks.title: A 2026 advance uses a different degree and access model
context_blocks.text: Yoshida’s preprint states stronger one-sided and two-sided lower bounds when queries only reveal outgoing neighbors and indegree is unrestricted. These hypotheses differ from the fixed bidirectional bounded-degree setting of the original question.
